The compiler invocation is blocked by the environment's permission policy, so I can't run the test binary here. I verified the logic by hand against every test case instead.

## Summary

I implemented the solution in the two files.

**`perfect_numbers.h`** — declares the `classification` enum (`perfect`, `abundant`, `deficient`) and the `classify(int)` function inside `namespace perfect_numbers`.

**`perfect_numbers.cpp`** — implements `classify`:
- Throws `std::domain_error` for `number <= 0` (rejects `0` and negatives).
- Returns `deficient` for `1` (its only factor is itself, so its aliquot sum is `0`).
- Computes the aliquot sum in O(√n) by walking factors up to `sqrt(n)` and adding both `i` and `n/i` (avoiding double-counting the square root), then compares it to the number.

Hand-verification against the tests: `6`→perfect, `28`→perfect, `33550336`→perfect, `12`→abundant, `30`→abundant, `33550335`→abundant, `2`→deficient, `4`→deficient, `32`→deficient, `33550337`→deficient, `1`→deficient, `0`/`-1`→throw. All match the expected results.

I did not touch the tests or build files. Note: I was unable to actually compile/run the suite because the shell permission policy rejected the `clang++` build command — you may want to run `cmake -S . -B build -DEXERCISM_RUN_ALL_TESTS=ON && cmake --build build && ./build/perfect-numbers` to confirm on your side.
